Tools that show their work

Every number comes with its formula and assumptions. Values in these demos are illustrative.

Model: illustrative pump, 3000 rpm and 10 in at full size. Speed and diameter use the affinity laws (flow scales with speed and diameter, head with their squares); trimming is an approximation. System curve: static head plus a flow-squared friction term, steeper as the valve closes. Power = flow × head × SG / (3960 × efficiency) in US units (gpm, ft, hp), or flow × head × SG / (367 × efficiency) in kW with flow in m³/h and head in m. 1 gpm = 0.2271 m³/h, 1 ft = 0.3048 m, 1 in = 25.4 mm. The operating-region band is a typical guideline, not a limit: use the vendor's allowable range.

Change the speed or the impeller diameter and see flow, head and power follow. Starting values are illustrative.

Calculation details (step by step)
Assumptions and limits
  • Fluid is treated as water (SG 1): hydraulic power = Q × H / 3960 in US units, with 1 hp = 0.7457 kW. Efficiency = hydraulic power / the rated shaft power you enter.
  • Speed and diameter ratios are combined into r = (N2/N1) × (D2/D1). Similar-efficiency point: Q = Q1 × r, H = H1 × r², P = P1 × r³.
  • The pump curve shape is generic, not your pump: head = H1 × (1.3 − 0.3x²) and power = P1 × (0.55 + 0.5x − 0.05x²), with x = flow / rated flow. Efficiency is derived from these two, so shutoff head is 130 % and zero-flow power 55 % of rated by construction.
  • System curve = static head + a flow-squared friction term fitted through the rated point. Static head must be below rated head. The new operating point is where the scaled pump curve crosses it.
  • Impeller diameter is limited to 95 to 100 % of full (a 5 % trim); the speed slider runs 50 to 120 %. A warning appears only for speed above rated.
  • Efficiency is taken from the scaled curve at the matching flow, so the extra loss from trimming is not modelled (the page notes that trimming typically lowers efficiency).
  • Not checked: NPSH, minimum flow, driver or motor limits, viscosity. Use the manufacturer curves for a real pump.

Q2 = Q1 x (N2/N1) x (D2/D1). H2 = H1 x (N2/N1)2 x (D2/D1)2. P2 = P1 x (N2/N1)3 x (D2/D1)3. Speed and diameter laws are applied one after the other. The system curve is static head plus a flow-squared friction term, set to pass through the rated point; the new operating point is where the new pump curve crosses it, so it differs from the simple affinity-scaled point. Efficiency at each matching point is held unchanged, which is a simplification: trimming typically makes the pump less efficient. The curve shapes are illustrative (head falls with flow, power rises with flow, efficiency is derived from them and peaks at the rated point); use the manufacturer curves for a real pump.

Sources: Pumps.org, trimming impellers (the equations and the Hydraulic Institute 5% statement and the effect on efficiency and power) and Pumps & Systems, impeller alterations (affinity rule is approximate).

Illustrative centrifugal compressor map. Change the speed, the impeller diameter (treated like speed, Q ∝ D and head ∝ D², as in the pump trim) or close the discharge valve and watch the operating point move toward the surge line. Starting values are illustrative.

Assumptions and limits
  • Ideal gas with Z = 1, no intercooling and no leakage. Gas k and MW come from a list of approximate values near 300 K, or from your own entries.
  • Polytropic head H = (R/MW) × T1 / a × (PRa − 1), with a = (k − 1) / (k × ηp). Discharge temperature = T1 × PRa. Gas power = mass flow × H / ηp, with density from the suction pressure and temperature (Z = 1).
  • The map is illustrative, not data for a real machine: head at flow ratio q is H × (1 + 0.35 × (1 − q²)), falling away faster above q = 1.15. Surge is fixed at 70 % and choke at 125 % of the flow at each speed; the surge control line is 10 % above surge flow.
  • Efficiency falls away from the design flow as η = ηd × (1 − 1.2 × (q − 1)²), never below 30 %.
  • Speed and impeller diameter are combined into one factor: flow scales with it and head with its square. The input boxes accept efficiency 40 to 95 %.
  • System curve = 30 % static head + 70 % flow-squared head, with the flow-squared part multiplied by (1 + 4 × valve closed %/100). With the valve open it passes through the design point.
  • Margin to surge = flow / surge flow − 1; margin to choke = choke flow / flow − 1. Warnings at under 10 % (surge) and under 5 % (choke) are illustrative thresholds.
  • Use the vendor map and surge control line for real work.

Model: ideal gas, compressibility Z = 1, no intercooling, no leakage. Polytropic head H = (R/MW) × T1 / a × (PRa − 1), with a = (k − 1) / (k × ηp). Discharge temperature T2 = T1 × PRa. Gas power = mass flow × H / ηp. Speed changes follow the fan laws: flow with speed, head with speed squared. The map shape, the surge line at 70% of design flow, the choke line at 125%, the constant-efficiency lines, the peak-efficiency line and the system curve (30% static, 70% flow-squared) are illustrative assumptions for teaching, not data for any real machine. Use the vendor map and surge control line for real work. Gas k and MW are approximate ideal-gas values near 300 K.

Illustrative reciprocating compressor. Pick the gas, set the cylinder size, speed, clearance and staging, and see capacity, volumetric efficiency, discharge temperature and power. Starting values are illustrative.

Rod gas load, first stage

Pulsation screening

Model: ideal gas, Z = 1, single suction conditions. Swept volume = π/4 × bore2 × stroke × cylinders × (1 or 2) × rpm (rod area ignored for double acting). Volumetric efficiency = 1 − C × (r1/k − 1), then multiplied by (1 − other losses). Isentropic discharge temperature T2s = T1 × r(k−1)/k; the tool estimates actual T2 = T1 + (T2s − T1) / η. Power per stage = mass flow × k/(k−1) × (R/MW) × T1 × (r(k−1)/k − 1) / η. Staging: equal pressure ratio per stage, intercooled back to the suction temperature, no pressure drop; the cylinder size is for the first stage. The clearance, losses and efficiency values are illustrative assumptions, not data for a real machine. For real design and limits (discharge temperature, rod load, pulsation) use the vendor data and API 618 (the reciprocating compressor standard for petroleum, chemical and gas industry services). Gas k and MW are approximate ideal-gas values near 300 K; natural gas varies with composition.

Rod gas load (first-stage cylinder, gas pressure only): compression load = Pd × Ap − Ps × (Ap − Ar); the opposite half stroke gives Ps × Ap − Pd × (Ap − Ar), negative meaning tension. Ap is the piston area, Ar the rod area. A single-acting cylinder is assumed to see atmospheric pressure (1.013 bar) behind the piston and never reverses. Inertia loads, valve pressure drops and pulsation are not included; the combined rod load check needs the vendor's reciprocating weights. Load reversal is commonly checked so that the crosshead pin is lubricated. Pulsation screening: speed of sound c = √(k × 8314 × T / MW); acoustic modes of a straight pipe are c/(4L) × (1, 3, 5, …) with one end open and one closed, or c/(2L) × (1, 2, 3, …) with equal ends; excitation is at multiples of the running speed, strongest at the cylinder pulse rate. Modes within ±20 % of a harmonic (an illustrative screening margin) are flagged. This is a first screening only: real pulsation and piping vibration studies follow API 618 and need an acoustic simulation.

Plant data: efficiencies and air flow are calculated

Enter what the DCS shows and get the actual overall efficiency at the generator terminals. Efficiency = electrical output ÷ (fuel mass flow × LHV). Compressor discharge pressure and fuel pressure are recorded, and CDP gives the pressure ratio; neither changes the efficiency.

Assumptions and limits
  • Efficiency = electrical output / (fuel mass flow × LHV), at the generator terminals and at today’s ambient conditions. It is not corrected to ISO. The result is only as good as the fuel flow, output and LHV you enter.
  • Fuel LHV (default 48 MJ/kg) and gas density for Nm³/h (default 0.75 kg/Nm³) are assumed values: replace them with your gas analysis. The tool does not define the reference conditions of an Nm³; it only multiplies by the density you enter.
  • Fuel pressure is recorded but not used in any calculation. Compressor discharge pressure only gives the pressure ratio shown (CDP / ambient; gauge readings have the ambient pressure you enter added).
  • Efficiency outside 15 to 45 % is flagged as unusual. An average exhaust temperature outside 500 to 560 °C is flagged (a range given by the expert, not a machine limit).
  • The four estimates (compressor efficiency, turbine efficiency, turbine inlet temperature, air flow) come from the same fixed constants as the model above: air cp 1.005 and k 1.40, hot gas cp 1.15 and k 1.333, inlet loss 1 %, combustor pressure loss 4 %, exhaust loss 1.5 %, combustion efficiency 99.5 %, mechanical and generator efficiency 98.5 %, no cooling air.
  • The compressor efficiency is the assumed value unless you give a discharge temperature. Estimates are not measurements. A turbine efficiency below 60 % or above 98 % is flagged.

The gas density and heating value are assumed natural gas values: replace them with your gas analysis. The estimate uses the same fixed assumptions as the model above (air cp from standard air-table values that rise with temperature, hot gas cp 1.15 and k 1.333, inlet loss 1 %, combustor pressure loss 4 %, exhaust loss 1.5 %, combustion efficiency 99.5 %, mechanical and generator efficiency 98.5 %, no cooling air). The result is the actual efficiency at today's ambient conditions. It is not corrected to ISO, because that needs the manufacturer's correction curves.

Generic what-if model (illustrative: here the efficiencies and air flow are inputs)

Simple-cycle gas turbine, ideal-gas Brayton model with losses. Change the ambient temperature or pressure, or the natural gas flow, and see power and efficiency. Starting values are illustrative, not a specific machine.

Assumptions and limits
  • Simple-cycle ideal-gas Brayton model. Air: cp 1.005 kJ/kg.K, k 1.40. Hot gas: cp 1.15 kJ/kg.K, k 1.333. Heat balance reference temperature 25 °C.
  • The air flow you enter is at ISO conditions (15 °C, 1.01325 bar) and is scaled with ambient density (pressure and 288.15 K / ambient temperature). Pressure ratio and the two isentropic efficiencies stay fixed at the values you enter at every ambient condition.
  • Losses: inlet 1 %, combustor pressure 4 %, exhaust 1.5 %, combustion efficiency 99.5 % (applied to LHV), mechanical and generator efficiency 98.5 % (applied to compressor-turbine net work).
  • Control mode: hold turbine inlet temperature (fuel is solved), or hold natural gas flow (the flow you enter is for ISO air flow and scales with the air flow). Turbine mass flow includes the fuel.
  • Not modelled: cooling air, steam injection, bleed, part-load control, the real compressor map, and any change of efficiency with ambient.
  • The comparison with ISO uses the same model at 15 °C and 1.01325 bar, not manufacturer correction curves. A turbine inlet temperature above 1700 °C is flagged. The chart sweeps ambient temperature from −10 to 50 °C or pressure from 0.7 to 1.05 bar.

Model assumptions (illustrative): air cp from standard air-table values that rise with temperature (1.005 kJ/kg.K at 300 K, 1.175 at 1200 K), hot gas cp 1.15 kJ/kg.K and k 1.333, air flow proportional to ambient density, fixed pressure ratio, inlet loss 1 %, combustor pressure loss 4 %, exhaust loss 1.5 %, combustion efficiency 99.5 %, mechanical and generator efficiency 98.5 %. Cooling air, steam injection, part-load control and the real compressor map are not modelled. Real ratings come from the manufacturer.

Steam turbine from steam properties (IAPWS-IF97 tables, interpolated). Set inlet and exhaust conditions and the isentropic efficiency. Starting values are illustrative.

Assumptions and limits
  • Steam properties come from a built-in table labelled IAPWS-IF97: 30 pressures from 0.02 to 200 bar, with superheated enthalpy and entropy every 10 °C above saturation (61 points). Values between table points are interpolated (logarithmic in pressure, linear in temperature); above the last point they are extended linearly.
  • Accepted inputs: pressures 0.02 to 200 bar absolute with exhaust below inlet, positive flow. The inlet steam must be superheated.
  • Single expansion with no extraction, leakage, governing loss or exhaust loss. Actual enthalpy drop = isentropic drop × the isentropic efficiency you enter, held constant at every flow and exhaust pressure.
  • Electric power = shaft power × mechanical and generator efficiency. Steam rate = steam flow / electric power.
  • Power against flow is a straight line (Willans line) that reaches zero at the no-load steam flow you enter (default 5 % of rated).
  • Exhaust dryness below 0.88 triggers a wet-steam warning; 0.88 is an illustrative threshold, not a design limit.
  • Use vendor curves for guarantees.

Power against flow follows a straight Willans line that reaches zero at the no-load steam flow (the no-load value is an assumption). Power against exhaust pressure keeps the isentropic efficiency constant, which is a simplification. Real turbines add extraction, governing losses and exhaust losses, so use the vendor curves for guarantees.

Weibull life model. The shape factor tells the failure pattern, the scale gives the characteristic life. Starting values are illustrative.

Assumptions and limits
  • Two-parameter Weibull for one failure mode, with no location (failure-free) period. MTBF = η × Γ(1 + 1/β), the Weibull mean. R(t) = exp(−(t/η)β). B10 = η × (−ln 0.9)(1/β).
  • Failure pattern bands: β below 0.95 infant mortality, 0.95 to 1.05 constant rate, above 1.05 wear-out. These bands are a working guide only.
  • Intrinsic availability = MTBF / (MTBF + MTTR). Operational availability adds the logistic and administrative delay per failure. The Weibull mean is used for every failure cycle, so treat availability as an approximation when β is far from 1.
  • Data fit: needs at least 3 times, all units failed (no suspended or censored units). Median ranks (Bernard, (i − 0.3)/(n + 0.4)) and a straight-line regression on the Weibull plot. R² is shown; no confidence bounds are calculated, so few failures give an uncertain estimate.

Estimate β and η from failure data

β below 1: failure rate falls with time (infant mortality or early life). β near 1: constant failure rate (random failures). β above 1: failure rate rises with time (wear-out). The 0.95 to 1.05 band is a working guide only. MTBF here is the Weibull mean, and the availability formulas assume a repairable item restored to service after each failure, so treat them as approximations when β is far from 1. The data fit uses median ranks (Bernard) and regression on the Weibull plot, and needs complete data without suspensions.

Check your asset against a reference value. The platform does not ship SMRP, OREDA or company numbers: enter the values from your own licensed copy or internal standard, and they stay on this device.

Your asset

Benchmark limits

Assumptions and limits
  • The tool contains no SMRP, OREDA or company values. The limits are whatever you type from your own source, and they are saved only in this browser, per machine type and source.
  • Machine type, failure mode and benchmark source are labels for your record; they do not change the calculation.
  • The check is pass or fail per metric: your MTBF at or above the minimum, your MTTR at or below the maximum, your availability at or above the minimum. There is no statistical uncertainty. A failure rate per 106 hours is converted to MTBF = 106 / rate, only when no minimum MTBF is entered.
  • Metrics with a missing value or limit are skipped. A benchmark is valid only if failure definition, equipment boundary and operating context match yours.

If you enter a failure rate, MTBF = 106 / rate. Benchmarks differ by definition (what counts as a failure, boundary of the equipment, operating context), so confirm that your data and the reference use the same definition before drawing conclusions. A single average also hides the failure pattern: use the Weibull tab for that.

Assumptions and limits
  • MTBF = operating hours / number of failures. MTTR = total repair hours / number of failures. Both are simple averages over the period, with no trend or failure pattern.
  • Intrinsic availability = MTBF / (MTBF + MTTR). Operational availability = MTBF / (MTBF + MTTR + delay per failure), where delay per failure = total logistic and administrative delay / failures.
  • Needs operating hours above 0 and at least one failure. The tool uses the hours exactly as entered: what counts as a failure and whether standby time is in the operating hours is your definition, so state it next to the result.

MTBF = operating hours / failures. MTTR = repair hours / failures. Intrinsic availability = MTBF / (MTBF + MTTR). Operational availability = MTBF / (MTBF + MTTR + delay per failure), where the delay covers waiting for parts, permits and crews. Definitions vary between organizations (what counts as a failure, whether standby time is included), so state the definition next to every result.

Series: R = R1 × R2 × ... Parallel: R = 1 − (1−R1) × (1−R2) × ... Both assume the parts fail independently over the same period. Values are illustrative.

Score each failure mode from 1 to 10. Agree the meaning of each scale, including the direction of the detection scale, before ranking: results compare only within one analysis.

RPN = Severity × Probability × Detection, as taught in the source course. Names and scores here are illustrative placeholders.

Practice

Case: high wheel space temperature after an outage

Sample case drafted from a course case study. Site and company names are removed. It needs the expert's review and a source-permission check before any public release.

What happened

Planned maintenance inspection completedA heavy-duty gas turbine is started afterwards.
Two wheel space channels read above alarmChannels 2AO-2 and 3FO-2 are above their alarm levels.
InvestigationThe as-found thermocouple insertion is checked against the insertion length stamped on the casing.
Finding and fixThe insertion was wrong. A step inside the thermocouple guide tube cap prevented correct insertion. After the cap was machined the thermocouples seated at the correct length.

Background from the course: wheel spaces are cooled by air flowing outward; excessive temperature is alarmed but does not trip the turbine; a bad thermocouple can raise a differential temperature alarm.

Built around a closed loop

Each real case becomes training. Each analysis becomes a documented decision. Each outcome returns to the library as new knowledge.

Our engineering principles

  • Every number shows its formula and assumptions.
  • Where data is missing, we say so instead of estimating.
  • No standard, limit or figure appears unless it is documented.
  • Real cases are anonymized and expert-reviewed before they appear.
  • This prototype stores nothing about you.
